What Should an Agency Test Before Showing a Website to a Client?

Follow a fictional Indian agency as it turns a rushed staging link into a clear review gate, issue log and client-ready presentation.

By SiteSutra · 09 November 2026

← All articlesYour next step ↓

Before an agency shows a staging website to a client, test three things in order: whether the build matches the approved brief, whether a visitor can complete the important tasks, and whether the release settings and ownership are ready for the next stage. If a blocker fails, return the site to the delivery loop instead of asking the client to discover it.

This is not a hunt for pixel-level preferences. It is an internal quality gate that separates delivery defects from the strategic or subjective feedback the client is actually qualified to give.

Aarav has a client call at 4 pm and an unreviewed link at 2 pm

Imagine Aarav runs a fictional Indian branding agency. The agency and project are original planning examples, not a SiteSutra client story or reported result. His white-label development partner sends a staging link for a professional-services website two hours before the client presentation.

The homepage looks polished at first glance. Aarav is tempted to forward the link immediately. Instead, he opens the signed-off brief and notices that one service is missing, the mobile menu covers the booking button, a successful test form reaches an old inbox, and the staging site still carries a search-blocking rule that must not reach production.

None of those issues needs client opinion. They need an owner, a severity and a retest. Aarav postpones the client link, records the four observations and turns the review into three gates.

Use three gates, not one vague approval

Aarav's hypothetical first-review gate
GateEvidence to inspectBlocker exampleDecision
1. Brief matchApproved sitemap, content, brand assets, component states and written scopeA sold service or required page is absentReturn for correction before client review
2. Visitor taskNavigation, enquiry, booking and other important flows on agreed devicesThe form appears to submit but no notification arrivesRepair, retest and attach evidence
3. Release hygieneOwnership, metadata, crawl rules, redirects, analytics boundaries and launch notesA temporary staging noindex rule has no documented removal stepAssign a launch owner and acceptance check

The gates answer different questions. Brief match asks whether the team built the agreed product. Visitor-task testing asks whether people can use it. Release hygiene asks whether the team can move it safely. Passing one gate does not compensate for failing another.

Gate 1: compare the build with the approved brief

Aarav reviews the staging site beside the signed-off source, not from memory. He checks the page list, page purpose, approved copy, supplied assets, form fields, integrations and exclusions. He also verifies that demonstration content and placeholder text have not become public-facing claims.

He records mismatches as observations: page, expected condition, actual condition and evidence. “It feels incomplete” is not actionable. “The approved tax-consulting service is absent from the services overview and navigation” can be assigned and retested.

Design differences belong here only when they depart from an approved direction or impair the task. New preferences discovered during review may be valid, but they should enter the agreed change process rather than being silently treated as defects.

Gate 2: complete the visitor's important tasks

Aarav chooses the small set of journeys the website was bought to support: find a service, understand fit, reach the contact option and complete an enquiry. He tests each journey on the devices and browsers agreed in scope. A browser list should be written before review; “works everywhere” is not a test plan.

For keyboard review, he starts at the address bar and uses Tab, Shift + Tab, arrow keys, Enter and Space. The W3C's Easy Checks advises checking that interactive elements can be reached, focus is visible, the order is logical and the user can leave every control without a keyboard trap. It also recommends inspecting page titles, headings, image alternatives, contrast, form labels and understandable errors. These quick checks are a starting point, not a claim of complete accessibility evaluation.

He submits the real staging form with test details and verifies the full chain: validation, successful delivery, honest confirmation, notification recipient and response ownership. A button animation or success message is not proof that the request arrived.

Gate 3: document release hygiene

Staging and production may require different settings. Aarav records which temporary restrictions must change, who controls the domain and hosting, what URLs need redirects, which canonical address each production page declares, and who can approve the release.

Google's site-move guidance tells site owners to check canonical links and robots meta rules, and to remove temporary noindex rules from new URLs when a move goes live. Google also explains that a sitemap can help discovery but does not guarantee indexing or increase ranking. The agency therefore treats these as release controls, not ranking promises.

The review separates analytics configuration from business outcomes. Aarav may verify that the agreed event fires after a successful action, but he does not call a click a qualified enquiry or promise that measurement will produce demand.

Classify findings before sending them back

Aarav uses a simple rule:

  • Blocker: prevents an important task, creates a serious release risk or contradicts a required deliverable. Resolve it before client review.
  • Major: materially weakens comprehension, usability or agreed quality but has a workable path around it. Assign it before presentation and decide whether it blocks the meeting.
  • Minor: a contained issue that does not stop the task. Record it; do not let it disappear into chat.
  • Preference or new scope: not a defect against the approved brief. Route it through the change process.

Severity describes impact, not how difficult the fix appears. A one-line configuration error can be a blocker; a time-consuming visual refinement can remain a preference.

Open each gate before the client link

Use these expandable prompts in the review call. They are intentionally short; the downloadable log holds the evidence and ownership.

Gate 1 — Does the build match what the agency sold?
  • Compare the live page list with the approved sitemap.
  • Check required content, brand assets, states and exclusions.
  • Search for placeholders, demonstration labels and unapproved claims.
  • Record each mismatch against the exact source decision.
Gate 2 — Can a visitor complete the important task?
  • Run the primary journey on an agreed small screen and desktop setup.
  • Use the keyboard for navigation, menus, controls and forms.
  • Submit real test data and verify delivery beyond the success message.
  • Test an invalid state and confirm the recovery instruction is clear.
Gate 3 — Can the team move towards release safely?
  • Confirm ownership and the named release approver.
  • Record staging-only crawl rules and the production acceptance check.
  • Review redirects, canonicals, sitemap and monitoring responsibilities.
  • Separate launch requirements from optional later improvements.

Keep one review log, not five message threads

Download the agency staging-review log (CSV). Replace the hypothetical observations with the real page, environment, expected condition, evidence, severity, owner and retest date.

Consolidate the agency's findings before sending them to the delivery partner. One issue should have one owner and one retest condition. Screenshots help with visual issues; short recordings help with flows; an inbox reference helps with delivery. Avoid collecting client names, personal form contents or credentials in the log.

Change the client meeting from bug discovery to decision-making

After the blockers are retested, Aarav sends a clean staging link with a focused agenda. The client reviews message accuracy, business fit, approved imagery and decisions that need their authority. They are not asked to act as the agency's form tester or release engineer.

The website can still produce new questions during client review. The difference is that known delivery defects have owners, the important journeys have evidence and the agency can distinguish a correction from a new request.

Make staging review a visible delivery stage

Aarav's agency does not need a large quality department. It needs a named reviewer, the approved brief, a small task list, a shared issue log and permission to stop the client link when a blocker fails. That routine protects the quality of the conversation as much as the quality of the build.
